notes:
I've written the notes below from the pages I was able to read. Two limits to keep in mind. First, the long verse-by-verse pages (Enduring Word, Ellicott) were cut off partway, so verses 24–34 rest on summary sections rather than full comments. Second, I found no material on these verses from Orthodox sources (oca.org), Lutheran, Methodist or Pentecostal denominational sites, or prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching, so those are left out.

## 1. The traditional reading, verse by verse

**v. 1:** Ellicott says this chapter and the next three form one long sermon preached to the crowds at the Temple. He thinks it fits King Jehoiakim's reign better than Josiah's. He links it to Jer 26, where the warning about Shiloh is dated to the start of that reign.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/7.htm

**v. 2:** Ellicott notes that as a priest, Jeremiah could go anywhere in the Temple.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/7.htm
- Guzik (Enduring Word) says preaching right at the gate took real courage. He quotes Ryken's view that it was probably a major festival, and says some think Jer 26 records the same sermon while others think it was a similar, separate one.  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-7/
- Matthew Henry: churchgoers need preaching as much as outsiders do.  https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jer/Jer_007.cfm

**v. 3:** Ellicott: "ways" means settled habits and "doings" means individual acts. The promise is that their present blessings will continue, not that they will get something new.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/7.htm
- Guzik: God offered to hold back judgment if they truly repented, in actions and not just words.  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-7/

**v. 4:** Ellicott thinks the threefold "temple of the LORD" was the false prophets' constant theme, or perhaps a chant in worship. The plural "these" covers the whole set of buildings.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/7.htm
- Henry calls the phrase "the cant of the times": people used it to calm themselves whenever they heard a warning.  https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/7-4.html
- Bible.org: in Hebrew, saying something three times expresses the highest degree. The people trusted the place of worship instead of the One worshipped.  https://bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-7
- Guzik shows how false prophets could have used Scripture to "prove" the Temple was safe: God's promise to David, His choice of Zion, and Jerusalem's escape from Assyria. Today's version, he says, is "I go to church."  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-7/

**v. 5:** Ellicott: "a man and his neighbour" is a Hebrew way of saying "one person and another."  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/7.htm
- Guzik reads this as a charge that Judah's courts were corrupt.  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-7/

**v. 6:** Ellicott: the foreigner, the fatherless and the widow are grouped as in Deuteronomy as the three standard examples of the helpless.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/7.htm
- Guzik: of the four signs of repentance listed, three concern how people treat each other. Quoting Thompson, he links "innocent blood" to judicial murders such as the one in Jer 26:23.  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-7/

**v. 7:** Ellicott: the Hebrew accents attach "forever" to the land God *gave*, not to the people's staying in it. The gift was meant to last, but their guilt forfeited it.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/7.htm (Guzik reads it differently; see Part 2.)

**v. 8:** Ellicott: the "lying words" are the slogan from v. 4.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/7.htm

**v. 9:** Ellicott: the Hebrew uses a series of infinitives, giving the sense of an outraged "What! Steal, murder…?"  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/7.htm

**v. 10:** Ellicott: the people left worship feeling "delivered", as if they had been set free *to* sin. Some versions instead read "Deliver us," mocking their prayer.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/7.htm
- Henry: those who keep sinning because grace has abounded in effect make Christ a servant of sin.  https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jer/Jer_007.cfm

**v. 11:** Ellicott: robbers hid in caves, and the worshippers, priests and prophets included, were using the Temple the same way. Jesus later used these words when He drove out the traders.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/7.htm
- Guzik: a robbers' den works in secret, but God says "I have seen it."  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-7/

**v. 12:** Ellicott: Shiloh was Israel's worship centre through the period of the Judges. It was corrupted, including by Eli's sons, lost the ark and fell into ruin.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/7.htm
- Guzik, quoting Ryken: archaeology shows Shiloh was destroyed twice.  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-7/

**v. 13:** Ellicott: "rising up early and speaking" is a phrase only Jeremiah uses, picturing God's eager effort. Jesus echoes "I called you" in Matt 23:37. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/7.htm
- Guzik: Judah's greatest sin was ignoring God's word, which left them without excuse.  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-7/

**v. 14:** Ellicott: this comparison with Shiloh, more than anything else, is what enraged the priests and people in Jer 26.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/7.htm
- Henry: God judges like cases alike.  https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jer/Jer_007.cfm

**v. 15:** Ellicott: people already knew the northern tribes (led by Ephraim) had been exiled, and Judah would share their fate. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/7.htm

**v. 16:** Ellicott: the command implies Jeremiah was already starting to intercede, as Moses did, and had to hold back.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/7.htm
- Henry: Jeremiah prayed because he didn't know the decree was final. Even when warning sinners, we should pray for them.  https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jer/Jer_007.cfm

**v. 17:** Henry: the sin was done openly, without shame.  https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jer/Jer_007.cfm

**v. 18:** Guzik: idolatry was a family affair. Quoting Cundall, the Queen of Heaven was the Babylonian Ishtar (Venus), probably brought in under Manasseh.  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-7/
- The commentaries collected on Bible Hub disagree on who she was: the moon (Gill, Abarbinel), a star (the Targum), the sun, moon and stars together (Geneva), or Venus/Ishtar (Cambridge). The Hebrew word for "cakes" is Assyrian-Babylonian and appears elsewhere only in Jer 44:19.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/7-18.htm

**v. 19:** Henry: their spite is aimed at God but can't harm Him. It harms only themselves.  https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jer/Jer_007.cfm

**v. 20:** Guzik: since they provoked God's anger, it will rightly be poured out on the land as well as the people.  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-7/

**v. 21:** Keil (on Bible Hub): this is irony. Their sacrifices mean so little to God that they might as well eat the burnt offerings too.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/7-21.htm

**vv. 22–23:** Keil: Jeremiah is thinking of the covenant at Sinai and the Ten Commandments, which say nothing about sacrifice. The point is not that God gave no law of sacrifice.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/7-21.htm
- Henry sums up the passage as "to obey is better than sacrifice."  https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jer/Jer_007.cfm

**v. 24:** Guzik: sacrifice carried on, obedience stopped. The human heart is not a reliable guide to pleasing God.  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-7/

**v. 25:** Bible Hub's study page: the Hebrew "again and again" (literally "rising early and sending") stresses God's continual effort to reach His people.  https://biblehub.com/study/chapters/jeremiah/7.htm

**v. 27:** Guzik's study guide: this repeats v. 13. The prophet's word was God's word and should have been treated that way.  https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/jeremiah/jeremiah-7.cfm

**v. 30:** Bible.org: this refers to idols set up in God's own Temple.  https://bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-7
- Restoration Commentary: Manasseh built altars to the stars in the Temple courts and put up an Asherah image.  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/onr/jeremiah-7.html

**v. 31:** Guzik (on Jer 19): unlike the Canaanite gods, the LORD never commanded human sacrifice. It was against His nature.  https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/jeremiah/jeremiah-19.cfm
- Gill: God never thought of it, still less desired or commanded it.  https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/nlt/jeremiah/7-31.html

**vv. 32–34:** Guzik: the valley will be renamed, bodies will lie unburied for the birds, and the sounds of joy and weddings will stop.  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-7/
- His study guide adds that judgment would make it seem all happiness and hope had left the land.  https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/jeremiah/jeremiah-7.cfm

## 2. Where Protestant teachers differ

None of these pages present their disagreements as denominational disputes. These are the real differences I found between Protestant commentators:

**v. 7 ("forever"):** Guzik says the verse shows God's land promise to Israel still stood 600 years after Joshua. He argues against those who say it was completely fulfilled under Joshua.  https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/jeremiah/jeremiah-7.cfm
- Ellicott instead stresses that Judah forfeited the gift. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/7.htm

**v. 16:** Guzik connects this to 1 John 5:14–16: there may be people beyond the reach of prayer. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-7/
- Henry stresses that Jeremiah prayed because he didn't know the decree was final. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jer/Jer_007.cfm

**v. 22:** Coffman rejects any critical reading that makes sacrifice unnecessary. God wants both holy living and the sacrifices He commanded.  https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/7-22.html

**v. 31 ("nor did it enter My mind"):** Don Stewart notes that open theists use this verse to argue God doesn't know the future. He rejects that, reading "heart" to mean God's intention, not His knowledge.  https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/stewart_don/faq/does-god-know-everything/19-was-god-unaware-that-the-people-would-build-high-places.cfm

## 3. Other views

**v. 10 (Protestant–Catholic):** Guzik says this isn't the same as later Catholic indulgences but shows "the same spirit." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-7/

**v. 18, Queen of Heaven and Mary:**
- Guzik quotes Ryken: calling Mary "Queen of Heaven" should alarm anyone who knows Jeremiah. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-7/
- GotQuestions: there is no queen of heaven, and the title has no scriptural basis for Mary.  https://www.gotquestions.org/Queen-of-Heaven.html
- John MacArthur (GTY) links Jer 7:18 to Catholic teaching on Mary in a sermon.  https://www.gty.org/sermons/90-315/exposing-the-idolatry-of-mary-worship-catholic-dogma-part-1exposing-the-idolatry-of-mary-worship-catholic-dogma-part-1
- The Catholic reply (Catholic Answers) says Jeremiah meant a pagan goddess, written centuries before Mary.  https://www.catholic.com/audio/ddp/queen-of-heaven-condemned
- It also says Jeremiah condemns offering *sacrifice*, which Catholics give to God alone, and that a counterfeit queen doesn't rule out a real one.  https://www.catholic.com/magazine/online-edition/is-there-a-queen-in-the-kingdom-of-heaven

**v. 18, modern scholarship:** Bible Odyssey has an article on the Queen of Heaven as one of the foreign gods Jeremiah condemned. I only saw its opening.  https://www.bibleodyssey.org/articles/queen-of-heaven/

**v. 22, modern scholarship:** The NET Bible note says some modern scholars use this verse to argue that the Pentateuch's sacrifice laws were written late, or that Israel didn't sacrifice in the wilderness. It prefers de Vaux's "dialectical negative": "not so much this as that."  https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=Jer+7:22-25
